item.title: Guam Veterans Day ceremony honors service while highlighting challenges facing veterans
item.description: Guam’s 2026 annual Veterans Day observance honored generations of military service while highlighting the ongoing need for accessible health care and support for the island’s veterans. The ceremony was held Wednesday at Gov. Joseph Flores Memorial Park at Ypao Beach. The observance brought together government officials, military leaders, veterans, and community members to recognize those who serve
item.content:encoded:
Guam’s 2026 annual Veterans Day observance honored generations of military service while highlighting the ongoing need for accessible health care and support for the island’s veterans.

The ceremony was held Wednesday at Gov. Joseph Flores Memorial Park at Ypao Beach. The observance brought together government officials, military leaders, veterans, and community members to recognize those who served in the U.S. armed forces and the families who supported them.

Keynote speaker Major General Esther J.C. Aguigui (Ret.), Guam’s Homeland Security Advisor, connected the island’s military contributions to its history, particularly the experiences of CHamoru families during the Japanese occupation in World War II.

Aguigui said Guam has more than 20,000 veterans, many of whom continue to face challenges accessing health care and Department of Veterans Affairs services. She noted that some veterans must wait for speciality care or travel to Hawaii for treatment unavailable on Guam.

“An island that gives the most has too often received the least,” Aguigui said.

She also called attention to women veterans who may not identify themselves as veterans or claim the benefits they earned through their service. Aguigui encouraged women who served in the military to recognize themselves as veterans and seek the care and services available to them.

“Since 1948, when women were first allowed to serve as permanent members of our armed forces, the daughters of Guam have answered the same call as our sons,” Aguigui said.

Aguigui outlines several efforts by the Leon Guerrero-Tenorio administration to improve veterans’ services, including advocating for a VA regional office on Guam, incorporating a veterans clinic into the planned Guam Medical Complex, and relocating the Office of Veterans Affairs to a new facility in Hagåtña.

She also highlighted efforts to digitize veterans’ records, train volunteer veterans services officers, and improve the Guam Veterans Cemetery in Piti. Those improvements include repairs to existing crypts and plans to add approximately 1,480 graves through a grant from the National Cemetery Administration.

Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero also addressed the gathering, recognizing the sacrifices made by veterans and their families. She connected Guam’s history of protecting its homeland to generations of residents who have served in the military and emphasized that honoring veterans should extend beyond the annual observance.

With approximately seven and a half weeks remaining in her administration, Leon Guerrero said her administration had worked to provide veterans with services they deserve and acknowledged the incoming administration for the Office of the Governor of Guam.

“I would like to recognize the Governor-elect Tony Ada and Lieutenant Governor-elect EJ Calvo, and I am very confident that I am leaving them in their hands a good administration that serves the people of Guam and our veterans,” Leon Guerrero said. “I am very confident that their leadership and their administration will continue that service moving forward.”

The ceremony also included a moment of silence for service members who died in service and veterans who have since passed away, as well as recognition of the 2026 Veterans of the Year for their accomplishments and leadership within their respective military organizations.

item.title: Chamorro lelek launch marks historic return of Saipan-built sakman
item.description: After nearly 500 years, a Saipan-built Chamorro sakman returned to Marianas waters Saturday morning as the traditional outrigger canoe Chamorro Lelek completed its maiden voyage from Susupe to Micro Beach with hundreds of spectators gathered along the shoreline. Community members, cultural practitioners, traditional navigators, elected officials and government leaders joined the Marianas Visitors
item.content:encoded:
After nearly 500 years, a Saipan-built Chamorro sakman returned to Marianas waters Saturday morning as the traditional outrigger canoe Chamorro Lelek completed its maiden voyage from Susupe to Micro Beach with hundreds of spectators gathered along the shoreline.

Community members, cultural practitioners, traditional navigators, elected officials and government leaders joined the Marianas Visitors Authority's Seafaring Traditions Program and the Commonwealth Council for Arts and Culture in celebrating the historic launch, which organizers said marked the first time in centuries that a Chamorro sakman built on Saipan had sailed in local waters.

The vessel's arrival at Micro Beach was greeted with cheers as crew members brought the canoe ashore during the Matatpanggen I Lelik/Afaifai launching ceremony honoring the maritime traditions of the Chamorro and Refaluwasch people.

John Castro, who helped lead the project through MVA's Seafaring Traditions Program, said the launch was as much about the future as it was about the past.

"So this canoe is finished, but we're not done," Castro said. "We want to keep sailing, and most importantly, we hope to inspire the next generation so it continues on. The only way we can keep our culture alive is to keep the practice going."

Castro said the project took more than eight years to complete after builders were forced to start over when an earlier canoe, carved from a log donated from Rota, was destroyed in a fire. Funding challenges, storms and limited manpower also slowed progress.

Despite the setbacks, Castro said the team remained committed to completing the canoe. "It looks like a canoe until we try it in the water," he said. "Then we can confirm if it is. Today, it is a canoe."

Among those aboard the sakman was master navigator Antonio "Tony" Piailug, son of legendary Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug. Piailug has spent the past several months training members of the Saipan seafaring group in traditional navigation and voyaging practices.

Piailug said the launch demonstrates that indigenous seafaring traditions remain alive and relevant today.

"If they want to continue, it's up to them," Piailug said of younger generations. "We try. If they want to learn, well, it's nice. For me, it's nice."

He emphasized that traditional navigation is inseparable from cultural identity.

"What we're doing is our culture. That's our identity," Piailug said. "If you know your culture, you know where you are from."

Piailug also said the sakman is designed as a voyaging canoe capable of traveling between islands, with the group hoping to attempt a voyage to Guam next year.

For organizers, the successful voyage of Chamorro Lelek represented more than the completion of a canoe project years in the making. It marked the revival of an ancient tradition that once connected the islands of the Marianas and signaled the beginning of a new generation of canoe builders, navigators and cultural practitioners dedicated to keeping that knowledge alive.

item.title: Guam Board of Education chair wants oversight hearing on Public Health's requirements for schools
item.description: Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division. Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms
item.content:encoded:
Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division.

Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms, but the department is merely complying with Public Health regulations.

She said the oversight hearing should be called, “with the goal of determining whether or not these regulations make sense. That is the source of many of the difficulties that we have experienced over the last few months.”

The Tiyan High School campus, which also housed students from Simon Sanchez High School, was closed by Public Health shortly after the school year began in August, leading to double sessions and emergency repairs.

She wanted the public to know the idea for cooler bathrooms did not come from the Education Department.

“People in the community don't understand this, that we have to honor those regulations, no matter whether or not they make sense,” she said, questioning whether air conditioning in restrooms would affect student learning. “I take great exception to the lack of clarification on the part of the media that do not understand where these regulations come from.”

She said air conditioning is also being installed at University of Guam restrooms.

“Can you imagine what the costs are going to be for DOE? We have to do this in every school, in every bathroom, and at the university and at GCC. Why could we not put ceiling fans? Would that not help?” she asked. “Split units, the cost of retrofitting the electrical requirements, the installation costs, the material costs, the equipment costs. I'd rather use that money in the classrooms.”

Because the matter could not be addressed during Monday’s emergency meeting for the department’s spending plan, Guthertz asked that it be placed on the board agenda for the upcoming Nov. 17 meeting.

The board will consider whether to ask the superintendent to request an oversight hearing on the Public Health requirements.

item.title: Federal government failed to hold Epstein accountable, Republican committee says
item.description: The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report Tuesday on its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates, concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors. "Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeated
item.content:encoded:
The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report Tuesday on its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates, concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said committee Chair James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky.

The scathing report comes after 15 months of interviews with 19 people, including former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton , Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick . Many of the interviews were conducted behind closed doors, with transcripts released days later.

Appearing in the Department of Justice's Epstein files or before the committee is not necessarily an indication of criminal wrongdoing.

The report found that the facts revealed by the investigation do not suggest President Donald Trump was implicated in any of Epstein's crimes . The report also accuses Democrats of launching an "unfounded witch hunt" by attempting to insinuate that Trump was involved in Epstein's crimes.

Epstein was arrested on federal sex-trafficking charges in 2019 and later died in prison. Authorities determined his death was a suicide.

In January, Democrats will take control of the House, with Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) expected to be at the helm of the committee. In a statement Tuesday, Garcia criticized the report as "partisan."

"Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein," Garcia said. "We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started."

Trump has long maintained he had a falling out with the disgraced financier before Epstein was indicted for soliciting prostitution in 2006. In February, White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson told NPR in a statement that "just as President Trump has said, he's been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein."

The report puts the next steps in the Epstein investigation into the hands of the DOJ, saying that the agency needs to interview or re-interview witnesses and investigate crimes committed by Epstein's associates. Maxwell is the only associate of Epstein to be charged with a crime and sentenced to prison.

In June , the committee interviewed Sarah Kellen, a longtime assistant of Epstein, who says she is also a survivor of his abuse. According to the committee's report, Kellen revealed the names of two men in her transcribed testimony that the committee sent to the DOJ for further investigation. The DOJ has not announced any investigations into the men.

The report concludes that if not for the "failures" of federal prosecutors in South Florida and Washington, Epstein's crimes after 2005 could have been prevented. Epstein's conviction in 2008 for soliciting sex from girls as young as 14 has long been criticized as a "sweetheart deal." Epstein served 13 months in Palm Beach County Jail with a 12-hour work release during the day . In addition, he had to register as a sex offender.

The report also says that "Epstein's pervasive influence and far-reaching connections" shielded him from further investigation. After Gates appeared before the committee in June , Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, called Epstein a "friend collector."

"He just liked to have people around him that were a big deal," Burchett said.

The report also says Trump's DOJ did not adequately communicate about the release of the Epstein files or protect survivors' personal information. The release was after the passage of the Epstein Transparency Act in 2025 and the release of millions of pages of documents. Large portions of the files were redacted, but the identities of many survivors were exposed.

Finally, the report concludes that some financial institutions failed to act on indicators of human trafficking and immigration fraud, enabling Epstein's activities. It said that the Treasury Department and its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network should review whether financial institutions are meeting their reporting responsibilities.

In a statement released Tuesday, the DOJ said Attorney General Todd Blanche has repeatedly said "the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."

"With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," the DOJ statement said of committee chair, James Comer. "The Department will continue following all additional investigative leads in matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein. Any victims with evidence and information are encouraged to reach out to the FBI."

The Treasury Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Garcia has promised that when the committee is under Democratic control that it will continue the investigation into Epstein with hearings open to the public.

Other Democrats, as well as some Republicans, have continued to push to hold Epstein associates accountable.

In September, the House of Representatives held billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying two congressional subpoenas. Between 2013 and 2017, Black paid Epstein millions of dollars. Black said the money was for tax and estate planning services, and he has since sued the committee and Comer to invalidate the subpoenas. Then, he sued Garcia for defamation.

item.title: House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
item.description: Updated November 11, 2026 at 12:08 PM ChST The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 11, 2026 at 12:08 PM ChST

The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

Tuesday's vote short-circuits any potential floor vote on the articles of impeachment, and virtually guarantees the measure will not be taken up before the current session of Congress expires.

The vote provided a surprise reprieve for President Trump's embattled Defense Secretary, who was facing an impeachment vote by the full House as early as Wednesday.

Massie reintroduced the articles of impeachment on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors in connection to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against Iran and on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's impeachment resolution sought to oust Hegseth over the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders.

Hegseth defended himself against the impeachment effort during a rare press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday, criticizing Massie as a "disgruntled and defeated congressman."

"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said. "I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow."

On Monday, Trump expressed support for Hegseth during a wide-ranging, impromptu press briefing at the White House.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

The impeachment measure was Massie's second attempt against Hegseth. He first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections , prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution again this week.

While the impeachment push may be quelled for now, Hegseth's troubles on Capitol Hill are not over. Democrats have promised vigorous investigations into Hegseth's Pentagon once they assume the majority in January.

Whether they will mount another impeachment effort remains unclear, but in an interview with NPR last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next Speaker of the House, said simply of Hegseth, "He's got to go."

item.title: Supreme Court seems split over federal agencies' ability to fine for law violations
item.description: At the Supreme Court, the justices seemed divided on Tuesday in a case that could undermine the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses that violate federal laws. For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers to pick crops.
item.content:encoded:
At the Supreme Court, the justices seemed divided on Tuesday in a case that could undermine the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses that violate federal laws.

For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers to pick crops.

In addition to wages, farm owners must provide basic necessities, such as housing, access to meals and water. The whole system is essentially policed by the Department of Labor to ensure that foreign workers don't undercut domestic laborers.

In that role, the department fined Sun Valley Orchards, based in New Jersey, a half-million dollars for unsanitary conditions, including providing unsafe drinking water, housing people in 20-bunk rooms, broken sinks and other violations, including failure to pay promised wages.

Sun Valley is disputing the charges and contends that the Department of Labor imposing monetary fines based on its administrative proceedings is unconstitutional. Sun Valley also says the process denies them the right to a jury trial when and if they appeal to a federal court.

At the high court Tuesday, Chief Justice John Roberts strongly suggested that the Trump administration, and many administrations before it, have exceeded the power of the executive branch. In this case, potentially wading into the judicial branch's territory.

Addressing Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who represented the Labor Department, Roberts said, "It seems to me you're just trying to leverage … the broad authority [of the executive branch] beyond the justification for its application."

Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked how disruptive it would be for the federal courts to enforce the law instead of the designated agency (in this case the Department of Labor).

Harris responded succinctly, "If the court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option."

Harris added that such a ruling would disrupt programs as diverse as Medicare, Medicaid, the federal student loan program and more.

That prompted this question from Justice Elena Kagan: "Why not just go to court always?" Harris quickly responded, "I think it would be catastrophic." She went on to explain that a system like that would inevitably result in massive under-enforcement of the law, given limited resources.

Lawyer Robert Johnson represented Sun Valley Orchards. "To be sure," he said, "the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated."

Johnson further contended that penalties should be imposed by the federal courts, not the administrative agencies that do most of that work under current law.

To that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson replied, "It seems like you're just sort of fighting the reality of … what Congress was trying to do … in ensuring that we don't have farm workers coming in and undercutting domestic workers."

A more skeptical observation came from Justice Brett Kavanaugh: "What you're proposing is really at war with clarity," he said, adding, "I think that's not great systematically going forward."

Justice Samuel Alito pointedly added, "What you're outlining is sort of a hodge-podge opinion, and maybe sometimes courts write that sort of thing," to which Justice Kagan quickly chimed in with a chuckling crowd in the court, "Not ever us!"

In rebuttal, Deputy Solicitor General Harris was unusually candid. "It would be a big deal for the government to lose, but an even bigger deal would be to have a mess," she said. She later added, "A lot of other statutory regimes also would be on the cutting-room floor."

And if that's the case, she said, the administration will have to go to Congress. Her voice rising, she added, "Please tell us now ... if we need to get Legislative Affairs on it right now, because this will snowball."

item.title: Russia's most famous independent newspaper has shut down after more than 30 years
item.description: Amid the war in Ukraine, the Kremlin has passed a web of wartime censorship laws. Those laws forced most independent Russian media to close or flee into exile. But there was one exception until this week, as NPR's Charles Maynes reports from Moscow. CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Duct tape on boxes...
item.content:encoded:
Amid the war in Ukraine, the Kremlin has passed a web of wartime censorship laws. Those laws forced most independent Russian media to close or flee into exile. But there was one exception until this week, as NPR's Charles Maynes reports from Moscow.

CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Duct tape on boxes...

MAYNES: ...Desks and chairs storage-bound and one final editorial meeting.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Non-English language spoken).

MAYNES: After more than 30 years, Russia's oldest and most famous independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, is closing. The publication a victim, say staff, of state pressure amid the Kremlin's war in Ukraine.

SERGEI SOKOLOV: (Non-English language spoken).

MAYNES: Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov announced the decision in a video last month, saying the Russian state had, quote, "killed" the newspaper, starving it of its ability to publish, raise money, rent an office or report without risk of prison time.

MAYNES: Founded in the early 1990s, Novaya Gazeta defended democratic ideals in Russia and criticized authorities when they fell short of them, sometimes at an excruciating cost.

UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: The body of Anna Politkovskaya was found...

ROBERT SIEGEL, BYLINE: She was a prominent critic of the war in Chechnya.

MAYNES: Six of its journalists were killed on the job, including star investigative reporter Anna Politkovskaya in 2006.

(SOUNDBITE OF PACKING MATERIAL RUSTLING)

MAYNES: On Monday, before cameras, staff remove portraits of all the slain journalists from an office memorial wall and carefully placed them into a box that simply read, ours - keep with care.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2021 to...

MAYNES: Novaya Gazeta's cofounder, Dmitry Muratov, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for the paper's defense of press freedoms, liberties that Muratov says are more under threat than ever.

MAYNES: "Repressions in Russia today are now sweeping in nature," he told a crowd of journalists outside the Novaya Gazeta office Monday, adding that Russia's security services effectively now ran the country. Following the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, this paper was one of the few independent media organizations to continue working inside Russia whose censorship laws forced other outlets and half of Novaya Gazeta's staff into exile.

TATIANA BRITSKAYA: (Non-English language spoken).

MAYNES: Novaya Gazeta journalist Tatiana Britskaya says, "yes, that's meant operating within certain limits." The trade-off, she says, has been worth it. Despite occasional criticism, the paper pulled punches.

BRITSKAYA: (Through interpreter) War is not just the battlefield. It's also refugees, political prisoners and people who are against the invasion but stayed. And in describing that, you really are talking about the war.

MAYNES: Meanwhile, pressure on the newspaper never went away. Muratov, the Nobel Prize-winner, was attacked and nearly blinded. The paper's office endured police raids, and all of its employees designated foreign agents, a connotation that hearkens back to Soviet-era enemies of the state.

MAYNES: Yet Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected charges the government had a role in Novaya Gazeta's demise. Amid a field of stiff competition, said Peskov, the closure was a standard, rational process - in other words, part of the media churn, an explanation Novaya Gazeta staffers reject.

ANDREI KOLESNIKOV: It's a slow strangulation of civil society here, and I feel it for a long time. This is not today's event.

MAYNES: Andrei Kolesnikov, a columnist for the paper, says he hopes the staff can find other ways to continue working together, adding they almost have no choice.

KOLESNIKOV: There is no job for people like us here in the circumstances of a totalitarian regime.

MAYNES: Yet, near him, Muratov was still at work.

MAYNES: As a crowd of Russian and foreign journalists gathered around, he held up pictures of Russian political prisoners, called for the evacuation of civilians and an end to bombings of Ukrainian cities. He also said, don't forget there are Russians, millions, who never wanted to attack their neighbor.

MAYNES: It was a defiant last act and a plea to keep the stories coming, even as his colleagues revealed a modified version of the newspaper's old office nameplate. It now reads - Novaya Gazeta lived here. Charles Maynes, NPR News, Moscow.

(SOUNDBITE OF MAZZY STAR SONG, "FADE INTO YOU") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.
